youtube.title: Payment System & Double-Entry Ledger Design: Staff-Level Reference Solution

description_top: The happy path of a payment is three boxes and a database. This question is about the other paths: a bank call that times out and leaves you not knowing whether the customer paid, three retries of the same payment at once, a refund ninety days later, and a statement that disagrees with your books. A full reference solution at the Staff bar (L6/L7): theory, a three-version design, eight challenges that break it, and the build cost. {DURATION} minutes, {SLIDES} numbered slides, with an interviewer, a candidate and a coach.

The thesis: exactly-once does not exist across a network boundary. So the design is at-least-once delivery, one effect per intent, a state for "we don't know yet", and a reconciliation that finds what the rest missed, all on an append-only double-entry journal where a balance is a sum, never a field.

IN THIS VIDEO
• Estimates as arithmetic: 40,000 journal entries a second, a hot merchant at 5,000 a second against one row lock, a 2-second budget the processor owns
• Theory: safety and liveness, seven mechanisms, an options matrix (including why a distributed transaction with the bank is impossible)
• Eight challenges: the bank timed out, three retries at once, a crash between ledger and event, the hot merchant, refunds and a late chargeback, 999,998 against 1,000,000, a bug that double-posted 40,000 entries, and how you would know
• The build cost and the one-way doors (marked AUX, the manager layer)

HOW TO USE IT
Run the round cold first. Then watch once straight through. On the second pass, pause after each interviewer question and answer it first. Slides badged AUX are the manager layer: skip them in a Staff round.

Not legal, accounting or compliance advice. The technical content has not been reviewed by a person.

post: Your payment call times out. Did the customer pay? "Mark it failed" is how double charges happen.

I've published a {DURATION}-minute reference solution for the payment system and double-entry ledger question, at the Staff bar: theory, a three-version design, eight challenges, and the build cost, on {SLIDES} numbered slides.

The idea that unlocks it: exactly-once does not exist across a network boundary. So you design for one effect per intent, a state for "we don't know yet", and a reconciliation that finds what everything else missed.

What it goes into:
→ A timeout is a state: UNKNOWN, then an inquiry by your own reference
→ Idempotency keys are inserted, not checked
→ A balance is a sum of immutable entries, never a column
→ Reconciliation is a component, not a safety net
Best on a second pass: pause after each question and answer it first.
It's a scripted walkthrough with synthetic voices, built with Claude Code from design-room, my open-source system design interview simulator.
When your books and the processor's disagree by two, where do you start?
